title: Why reviewing AI code is a bottleneck (and how to fix it)
author: Jigar Prajapati
summary: We’ve all been there. You give Cursor, Claude Code, or an autonomous agent a prompt. It thinks for 20 seconds and spits out a 500-line diff across 12 files. You scroll through it. It looks like code. The tests pass. You hit "Approve" and move on. But a recent study by JetBrains and UC Irvine found something terrifying: developers using AI assistants actually switch contexts more frequently, and 74% of developers didn't notice this increase. We are writing code faster than we can actually review it. The cognitive load of verifying AI output is quietly accumulating, and it's leading to a new kind of technical debt: The "Blind Merge." We don't need AI to review AI. We need a fast, deterministic way to know where to look first. I wanted a tool that would read my git diff and just tell me: "Hey, you touched the auth folder, and you deleted two test lines. Look here first." So I built risk-annotate. It’s a completely local, zero-dependency CLI. No cloud, no telemetry, no API keys. It runs on any diff and annotates the riskiest hunks. Here is what it looks like running on a recent commit: # Risk annotations `HEAD~1..HEAD` · 7 files · 3 HIGH · 3 MED · 1 LOW ## `src/a.test.ts` - L1-1: [HIGH] Removes 2 test lines; confirm coverage was not dropped to make the suite pass (path heuristic) ## `src/auth/login.ts` - L5-5: [HIGH] Touches auth code; check session, token and permission handling (path heuristic) ## `.github/workflows/ci.yml` - L1-1: [MED] CI workflow changed; check permissions, secret usage and triggers (path heuristic) ## `package.json` - L5-6: [MED] Adds new dependency "zod"; review provenance, license and maintenance (dependency manifest)

title: Robotic therapy for stroke patients
author: Ashish
summary: 弱視トレーニングは「続かない」が最大の敵だった——AI×ロボットのリハビリ報道から考える、VRゲームという選択肢 1. きっかけは、リハビリの「人手不足」ニュース MIT Technology Reviewが報じた「Robotic therapy for stroke patients」。 脳卒中を起こした人のうち、毎年500万人が長期的な障害を抱えている。しかし理学療法士の数は足りず、必要なケアに行き渡らない。そこで注目されているのが、AIと人間のセラピーを組み合わせる新しいアプローチだ。元MITポスドクで現在は助教を務めるJohannes Lachner氏らの取り組みが紹介されている。 このニュースの本質は「ロボットが療法士を置き換える」ではない。 反復トレーニングという、地味で、量が必要で、どうしても続かない工程を、テクノロジーが支える という点にある。 そしてこの論点は、視覚のトレーニングにもほぼそのまま当てはまる。エンジニアとしてこの記事を読んだとき、僕が最初に思ったのは「これはリハビリのUX問題だ」ということだった。 adherence（継続率）が低いのは、患者の意志が弱いからではない。 フィードバックループが遅く、報酬が遠く、退屈だという設計の問題 だ。だったら、その設計を組み直せばいい。 2. 弱視（lazy eye / amblyopia）の訓練が抱えるジレンマ 弱視や関連する両眼視の問題に対して、長く使われてきたのがアイパッチによる遮蔽だ。優位眼を隠し、弱い目を単独で使わせる。理屈は明快で、実績もある。 ただし、現実には次の壁がある。 子どもにとって地味で、大人にとっても退屈。継続が難しい 「片目を隠す」訓練なので、両目を同時に使う力（両眼視）を直接は鍛えない 家庭で毎日一定量をこなすには、モチベーションの設計が要る つまり、リハビリと同じ「継続の問題」を抱えている。ここで一度、システムとして整理してみる。弱視訓練を「入力（視覚刺激）→ 処理（脳の両眼統合）→ 出力（日常動作）」というパイプラインとして見ると、従来の遮蔽は 入力段で片眼を落とす 操作にあたる。一方、両眼視の再学習は 処理段の再配線 を狙うもので、必要な刺激の出し方が根本的に違う。この違いを、家庭のリビングでどう再現するか——それが設計課題になる。 3. そこで、反復をゲームにする Seven SportzがMeta Quest向けに開発した AmblyoPunch は、この「継続」にゲームの力でアプローチするVRトレーニングゲームだ。 ゲームの基本はシンプル。飛んでくるガボールパターン（縞模様）のコインを、コントローラーやハンドトラッキングでパンチして得点にする。赤いトゲが迫ってきたらよけてかがむ。ハートは3つ、すべて失うとリスタート。ワールドは村から都市、宇宙、月、火星、金星へと進み、オブジェクトは速く、小さくなり、トゲは大きくなる。 単なる的当てではない。裏側に4段階のダイコプティック（両眼分離提示）設計がある。 Stage 1 単眼ウォームアップ — ターゲットを弱い目にのみ提示 Stage 2 抑制の解除 — 優位眼の映像を強く暗く／白っぽくし、抑制をゆるめる Stage 3 再バランス — 明瞭さを徐々に回復させ、両眼の寄与をそろえる Stage 4 融像トレーニング — Panumの融像領域内のわずかなずれを与え、1つの3D知覚に統合する練習 進行はパフォーマンスでゲートされる。直近10回の結果でおおむね70%以上、斜視（strabismus）のプロファイルでは最終融像の前に80%以上が目安とされている。 エンジニア目線で面白いのは、これが 適応型の難易度制御（adaptive difficulty） になっている点だ。ゲームの世界では、プレイヤーのスキルに合わせて敵の強さを動的に変える仕組みが当たり前になっている。AmblyoPunchはその考え方を、視覚刺激の提示パラメータにそのまま流用している。閾値に近い負荷をかけ続けることで、学習を最大化しようという発想だ。直近10セッションの窓で成功率を見るのは、ノイズの多い単発結果に引っ張られないための 移動平均的な平滑化 だと読める。 Stage 2の「優位眼を暗くする」処理も、技術的には興味深い。片眼に強い信号、もう片眼に弱い信号を同時に提示し、脳が強い方だけを見て弱い方を無視する 抑制（suppression） をゆるめにかかる。VRの両眼分離レンダリングがあるからこそ、左右の目に別々の映像をフレーム単位で出し分けられる。専用ハードなしでこれが家庭に届くのは、Questというプラットフォームの恩恵だ。 4. 「あなたの目」に合わせる設定 同じ弱視でも、弱い目が左右どちらか、重症度、斜視のタイプは人によって違う。AmblyoPunchはそこを設定で合わせる。 弱い目: 左 / 右（逆に選ぶと効果が反転するため、ここは正確に） 重症度: 軽度 / 中等度 / 重度 → ターゲットのサイズ、速度、ステージの長さが変わる 斜視: 内斜視 / 外斜視 → Stage 4の視差・輻湊シフトが変わる 基本は 自動モード が推奨で、カスタム（手動での単眼／両眼提示、融像トグルの操作）は上級者向けだ。 設定項目を並べてみると、これは一種の キャリブレーション・パラメータ だとわかる。弱い目を「左/右」で切り替えるのは単なる左右反転ではなく、刺激を届けるチャネルの選択だ。逆に設定すると、鍛えたい目ではなく優位眼をさらに強化してしまう。重症度プリセットはターゲットのサイズ・速度・ステージ長をまとめて調整する。つまり「難易度カーブの初期値」を症状に合わせて差し替えているわけだ。手動カスタムを上級者向けに置いているのも妥当で、誤った融像トグルは学習を妨げかねない。 5. 日常の自信につながるか セッションを終えてヘッドセットを外したあと、ボールを受け止める、階段を降りる、奥行きを使って手と目を協調させる——そうした日常動作に自信が持てるかどうか。 訓練が「続けられる」ことは、効果を語るうえでの前提条件だ。好きなコンテンツで毎日触れる設計は、その前提を満たすための現実的な答えのひとつだと思う。ゲームとして「もう1回」と思えること自体が、リハビリ文脈では大きなアドバンテージになる。報酬ループを内側に持つ設計は、外から「やらされる」訓練より、長い目で見て持続しやすい。 6. 大事な注意点 AmblyoPunchはトレーニング／支援型のゲームであり、 医療機器でも治療でも治癒でもない 。専門家による眼のケアの指導を補助するもので、決して置き換えるものではない。臨床的な判断は、必ず眼科医や視能訓練士などの専門家に相談してほしい。 そのうえで、リハビリの世界で起きている「反復をテクノロジーで支える」という流れが視覚トレーニングにも届くなら、選択肢は確実に増える。エンジニアとして言えるのは、これは派手なブレークスルーではなく、 地味な設計改善の積み重ね だということ。両眼分離レンダリング、適応型難易度、症状別パラメータ——どれも既存技術の組み合わせで、そこがむしろ強い。続かないという最大の敵に、設計で立ち向かう。その姿勢に、僕は少し希望を感じている。 製品ページ（Meta Quest）: https://www.meta.com/en-gb/experiences/amblyopunch/1239507485902689/

title: OpenAI Beelzebub Linux Simulation with Custom Wazuh Detection Rules
author: james chambers
summary: Intro I set out on this lab to learn how to set up a honey pot and how to connect it to SIEM. I choose a honeypot called Beelzebub that can emulate real shell responses to attackers by querying OpenAI with an API key. The SIEM I am using is Wazuh for it's customization and flexibility. Using Wazuh will allow me to write custom rules that will send alerts for 3 different attacker simulations I want to run on Beelzebub. The attacks I am going to carry out is a TCP port scan, a brute force attack, and running Linux shell commands over ssh. I want to thank the developers of Beelzebub for making this awesome open source tool and I also want to give a massive thanks to Taylor Walton, whose article I used as an outline for my lab. Before we get into it a little about me. I have been studying cybersecurity for a little over 3 years now. I seen the blind spot that people have for security on the internet and I want to help fill the role of protecting. I am always looking to help others and cybersecurity is a really good way to protect others. Setup Before I can jump into using Beelzebub I need to make sure I meet all the prerequisites. I met all except Docker was not installed yet. Once I had Docker installed I could start my journey with Beelzebub. I started by getting a clone of the Beelzebub-labs and then ran './install.sh --docker'. Once I had confirmed docker was up and had recorded a log I shut down docker using 'docker compose down' and I had quite a few configurations I needed to add/edit. I used Beelzebub ssh for port 2222 since I was using ssh port 22 to run the machine I was on. This also created a problem when I first tried launching all the Beelzebub instances. It tried running on ssh on port 22, among many other things, but since the Linux machine was using it, it failed to launch. I had to go into 'beelzebub.yml' and remove port 22 from the configuration so it would finally work. Once I had figured that out, I moved on to configuring the ssh 2222 Yamal file to respond as if it were an actual instance of Linux. I ran into a bump here where I could connect to Beelzebub via ssh but I would not get any responses when using commands. This was quite annoying, but, after combing back through everything a few times, I found a couple of mistakes I had made. First, I had not correctly copied the API key so I basically had no key at all. Second, I figured out needed to pay a small fee to get the API keys to respond from OpenAI. Now $5 poorer, Beelzebub finally responded to my Linux commands. Pretty awesome to see Beelzebub responding as if I had connected to a real instance of Linux. I wasn't quite done just yet though. I needed to set up a Wazuh agent on the machine to forward logs to the SIEM. Once I had installed the agent I needed to tell the agent where to get the logs from. I needed to change 'beelzebub.yaml' to save the logs to a text file. I ran into more trouble here but it was a typo. I had misspelled one of the words by one letter in the configuration file and I just couldn't find it for the longest time. When I finally realized what I had done, I felt so dumb. On the bright side though it did cause me to be much more cautions and I did not make another typo for the remainder of this lab... I'm sure I will eventually make this mistake again. With all the configurations now spelt the right way, I was finally getting logs in my SIEM from Beelzebub. On to the attacks!!! Simulating Attacker Behavior PORT SCAN The first attack I wanted to see Beelzebub detect was a stealth scan... Until I realized it couldn't detect it. I could not get Beelzebub to detect the stealth scan but I could get it to detect a TCP port scan. I pivoted to making a Wazuh manager rule for TCP traffic instead. This rule will detect a new TCP session and send an alert to the Wazuh SIEM that says "Possible TCP port scan." I know this isn't exactly the best way to detect a TCP port scan but for this lab this is enough for a proof of concept. I was a little frustrated I couldn't get a better alert for this attack but my other attempts kept ending in failure. I did however get an alert to go off when new TCP sessions were created which is a good start to me. (Wazuh events of TCP traffic) BRUTE FORCE (METASPLOIT) Any excuse to use Metasploit is a welcome one for me. One of my early memories of getting into cybersecurity is using Metasploit to hack into other computers in labs. Of course I could've just manually typed in multiple different passwords at random... but where's the fun in that. First though, I configured a few new alerts for the Wazuh manager. Now that Wazuh will send alerts for the login attempts it was time to use Metasploit. I went to the 'ssh_login' and set up all the values I needed. I created my own password list and made sure I was trying this over port 2222. Then I ran the command and let it try all the passwords for me. (values set for Metasploit ssh_login) Unfortunately for me Metasploit could not create an actual session so my time with the tool was over but it had created the traffic I needed to have logs pop up in my SIEM. (Metasploit output.) (These are all logs of failed login attempts along with one successful one.) RUNNING COMMANDS The final attack I wanted to do is to run commands over ssh. This was partly because I wanted to see how Beelzebub would respond to different commands. Just like all the others I started by making the rule for the Wazuh manager. I then ran a few commands to generate some logs. The commands I ran were the same as the image I posted earlier in this blog. It was really cool to see it spit out so believable responses. I then went over to the Wazuh SIEM and found all the logs of the commands I ran. (logs of commands executed) I feel very acomplished in this lab. First of all, I actually got Beelzebub working. Then I moved on to an attackers point of view. I scanned for open ports I could connect to. Then I tried using Metasploit to brute force over ssh into the Beelzebub honeypot. Once I got a password, I used ssh over a normal shell to connect to Beelzebub and run commands on it. I also created rules that would trigger alerts to Wazuh. I was able to successfully receive alerts from each simulated attack proving my amazing new rules worked. I went too fast at times and made some silly mistakes like typos but this also taught me how careful I have to be with editing configuration files. I also learned that sometimes the answer is just a couple of bucks. I also learned that Beelzebub can't capture every kind of scan which helped show me the importance of having multiple defenses in place. The End I enjoyed messing with Beelzebub and Wazuh. I had fun figuring out how to customize my own alerts using Wazuh rules. It was also cool to use AI to simulate a fake Linux shell to attackers. I wish I had been more careful when editing the configuration files. It also would've help to really take on the challenge one step at a time. There were multiple times during this lab that I thought something else was broken when really it was that typo or the API key being wrong. I wouldn't have been able to do this with out Taylor Walton. He wrote an excellent article on Medium and even made a video to go along with it. It was immense help during this lab and I often found myself referencing it when things went wrong. Refrences Beelzebub, Open-source deception framework Beelzebub This helped me download and start beelzebub. https://github.com/beelzebub-labs/beelzebub/blob/main/README.md Install Docker Engine on Ubuntu Docker This helped me install the prerequisite DOCKER for Beelzebub. https://docs.docker.com/engine/install/ubuntu/#install-using-the-repository Wazuh rule for ssh traffic ( I used as an example and then wrote my own ) Taylore Walton, SOCFortress Sep 23, 2025 This was the original rule used in the Medium article that I used to test if my beelzebub was forwarding logs correctly. https://github.com/socfortress/Wazuh-Rules/blob/main/Beelzebub/100660-beelzebub.xml Deploying an AI Honeypot with Beelzebub + OpenAI Taylor Walton, SOCFortress Sep 28, 2025 This was my main guide during the lab. From setup to configurations this was the piece that showed me in steps how to use the beelzebub tool. https://socfortress.medium.com/deploying-an-ai-honeypot-with-beelzebub-openai-smarter-traps-for-smarter-attackers-d86552d35a9e Rules Syntax Wazuh This was the piece that helped me to create all the different rules for Wazuh. https://documentation.wazuh.com/current/user-manual/ruleset/ruleset-xml-syntax/rules.html#rules-field TCP Connect Scan Nmap This helped me to run the correct command and how I could modify it with flags. https://nmap.org/book/scan-methods-connect-scan.html Active Scanning MITRE ATT&CK This was the attack technique I was simulating. https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1595/ Vulnerable Application Dwelch-r7, h00die, james, zeroSteiner, cnotin Feb 23 2017 This helped me navigate Metasploit and helped me use the right auxiliary. https://github.com/rapid7/metasploit-framework/blob/master/documentation/modules/auxiliary/scanner/ssh/ssh_login.md Brute Force MITRE ATT&CK This was the attack technique I was simulating. https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/ Command and Scripting Interpreter: Unix Shell MITRE ATT&CK This was the attack technique I was simulating. https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/004/

title: 5 AI Coding & Builder Tools You Can Actually Use for Free (Oct 2026)
author: Tool Use Cases (Lali Publications)
summary: Most AI developer tools ask for a credit card before they let you build anything real, or hide their actual model restrictions in pricing footnotes. At Tool Use Cases , we track AI tools by the specific job you need done and verify each tool's pricing and free tier directly against its official docs and pricing pages. Here are five AI coding and builder tools you can start using for free right now in October 2026—matched to the one job each is best at, plus an honest verdict on when not to use it. 1. Vibe coding a real codebase: Cursor The job it fits: Building and iterating on a real repository where you want full IDE control while the AI writes and edits most of the code. What's free (checked Oct 22, 2026): Free plan with limited agent use—enough to test it on a real project before paying. Pricing caveat worth knowing: Since October 2026, Cursor is sold as part of The X Subscription. The $8/mo Plus tier runs only Cursor's own models (Grok, Composer); cloud agents and frontier models from Anthropic (Claude) or OpenAI (GPT) start on the $30/mo Premium tier and are billed at API list price. When NOT to use it: If you want a flat $20/mo subscription that includes frontier models from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google inside your editor—compare Devin Desktop (formerly Windsurf) at $20/mo Pro first. If you don't want to manage local dev setup or git at all and just want a prompt-to-full-stack web app in a browser tab (use Lovable , Bolt.new , or Google AI Studio instead). Compare alternatives: Best AI for vibe coding 2. Prompt-to-web-app in the browser: Google AI Studio (Build mode) The job it fits: Going from a plain-English prompt to a working web app in the browser with one-click deployment to Google Cloud Run. What's free (checked Oct 23, 2026): Google states AI Studio is free to use with a Google account, with paid tiers only when you scale to heavy traffic or paid Cloud Run usage. When NOT to use it: If you need built-in user authentication and a Postgres database wired up out of the box from your first prompt— Lovable (free plan: 5 build credits/day, up to 30/month) or Bolt.new (free plan: 1M tokens/month) are purpose-built for full-stack Supabase/auth scaffolding. Note for Google Cloud users: skip Firebase Studio for new projects—it closed to new sign-ups on June 22, 2026 and shuts down on March 22, 2027. Compare alternatives: Best AI for vibe coding 3. Delegating GitHub repo tasks to an async agent: Google Jules The job it fits: Handing off well-scoped bug fixes, tests, or small features to a background agent that clones your GitHub repo and opens a pull request for you to review. What's free (checked Oct 23, 2026): Free beta with up to 15 tasks a day . (If you prefer an interactive agent-first editor + CLI, Google's Antigravity also has a $0 individual plan with weekly rate limits.) When NOT to use it: When you're doing heavy, interactive multi-file refactoring from your own terminal where the agent needs to run local test suites in a tight loop. For serious paid agentic work, Claude Code (requires Claude Pro at $20/mo or Max; not on the free plan) remains our top pick, and OpenCode (MIT license) is the best free open-source terminal alternative if you want to bring your own models. Compare alternatives: Best AI coding agents 4. Prototyping a playable browser game: Rosebud AI The job it fits: Turning a prompt into a playable 2D or 3D browser game (Phaser / Three.js) in minutes, or remixing existing community games to test a mechanic. What's free (checked Oct 22, 2026): The free plan starts you with 8,000 credits, no credit card required (paid Pro plan is $50/mo). Google's Gemini Canvas and AI Studio Build mode are also free for quick browser game tests. When NOT to use it: When you're building a commercial game in a full engine like Godot, Unity, or Unreal —use Cursor alongside your engine instead so you own a standard project structure. When you need style-consistent commercial 2D art assets ( Scenario handles style consistency, though its free tier is for personal/evaluation use only) or 3D meshes ( Meshy gives 100 free credits/month). Compare alternatives: Best AI for game prototyping 5. Running open-weight models locally: Ollama The job it fits: Downloading and running open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, DeepSeek, etc.) on your own machine with a single command ( ollama run ... ) and a local HTTP API. What's free (checked Oct 23, 2026): Free and open source ( MIT license ). The only cost is your own hardware. Pair it with OpenCode for a 100% local, offline coding agent. When NOT to use it: If your laptop has 8–16 GB of unified memory and you expect frontier-level multi-file coding reasoning at high speed. Small local quantizations are great for offline drafts, privacy-sensitive data, and local embeddings/RAG, but they won't match hosted frontier models on complex architecture changes. Compare alternatives: Best tools for running AI locally Two builder updates from this week worth knowing Replit Monitoring Agent (shipped Oct 23, 2026): Replit's Agent can now watch your published app's logs and alerts in the background, investigate production issues, and test a fix. By default, you review and publish the fix yourself unless you opt into the experimental Auto-republish setting. Replit also added an overage buffer for eligible top-up customers so published apps don't immediately go dark when credits hit zero. Our verdict: This addresses the scariest part of shipping a vibe-coded app—what happens when it breaks in production—but keep Auto-republish off until you've seen how it behaves on your app. ( Replit Oct 23 changelog · Best AI for fixing broken code ) Lovable auto-creates and connects Supabase projects (shipped Oct 20, 2026): If your Lovable app doesn't have a backend yet, Lovable can now provision and wire up a Supabase project directly. You pick the organization and region (note: the region cannot be changed later), and Supabase bills that project to your own account.
